title: Lift the self by the self
hookLine: Arjuna sank down in his chariot; chapter six says the self that sinks you can lift you
carry: lift the self by the self
tomorrow: A clean place, a firm seat
last: SHANTI — LASTING PEACE COMES FROM THE FRIEND OF ALL BEINGS THAT DOESN'T END.

lines: HIS BOW SLIPS FROM HIS HAND.
HE SINKS DOWN IN THE CHARIOT.
WHAT DOES YOUR OWN VOICE SAY?
cards: Go back to the very start of the Gita. Two armies face each other. Arjuna, a great archer, looks across and sees his teachers, his cousins, his grandfather.
His bow slips from his hand. He sinks down onto the seat of his chariot and says he won't fight. Everything Krishna teaches after that is an answer to that sinking.
Now listen to the voice in your own head after something goes wrong. You always do this. What's wrong with you.
Words you'd never say to a friend. Chapter six has two lines about that voice too.

teach.b: First, Krishna clears something up. The true renouncer, verse one says, isn't the one who stops lighting the sacred fire or stops working. It's the one who does what needs doing without leaning on the fruit.
For someone climbing toward yoga, verse three adds, action is the way up; for someone who has arrived, stillness. Then verses five and six.
Lift yourself by yourself; don't let yourself sink.
For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self. In Sanskrit the same word, atman, the self, comes again and again, like a mirror facing a mirror.
The word for friend is bandhu: a friend, and also kin. Here's the Hindu teaching under it.

teach.h: YOU ARE NOT YOUR WORST MOMENT.
teach.b: You are not your worst moment.

teach.h: LIFT THE SELF BY THE SELF.
teach.b: Many teachers read the verse as the higher self lifting the lower, the steady mind lifting the scattered one. The verse doesn't say wait to be rescued, and it doesn't say you're alone; later chapters speak of grace.
It says the lifting starts with your own hand. Then a portrait of the one who has done it: steady in cold and heat, praise and blame. A lump of earth, a stone and gold look alike to them.
So when the inner voice piles on after you slip, the Gita's question is simple: which self is talking, the one sinking you, or the one lifting you?

how: Gita 6.5 ('uddhared atmanatmanam', lift the self by the self) is often learned by heart, and some Hindus recite it as encouragement in hard times.

o: a friend who is also kin
a teacher who guides the self

games.q: what's inside the verses — tap the pairs.
p: the way up, for the one climbing
the way, for the one arrived

s: the true renouncer, in 6.1, stops doing any work
it's the one who does what needs doing without leaning on the fruit.
verse 5 says the self can be its own friend and its own enemy
the self alone is friend of the self, and the self alone its enemy.
to the one who has mastered the self, gold matters more than stone
verse 8: a lump of earth, a stone and gold look alike to them.

games.q: you slipped, and the inner voice is piling on. by Gita 6.5–6.6, what's going on?
o: the self is acting as its own enemy; the same self can lift you.
the voice is a second, evil self you have to obey.
the voice is right: being harsh is how you lift yourself.
games.why: the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone its enemy. the lifting starts with your own hand.

practice: Say the first words of verse five softly, out loud: uddhared atmanatmanam. Lift the self by the self. Now think of the last time the inner voice was harsh with you, and let the words come up.
Imagine a good friend heard them said about you, and let the friend's answer come, warm. Say the line once more, and let that be the voice that answers.

wordCard.voice: Bandhu. Friend, kin: the self is its own bandhu. Gita six, five: the self is the friend of the self, and the enemy of the self. The lifting starts with your own hand.

orig.note: Sanskrit: bandhu, friend or kin; from a root meaning to bind. the self is its own bandhu (6.5).

carryVoice: Your line: lift the self by the self. The harsh voice doesn't get the last word. Day one hundred seventy-eight.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 1.29–1.30, 1.47 (Arjuna's bow slips; he sinks down on the chariot seat)
